source.title: Register Always Matters: Analysis of LLM Pretraining Data Through the Lens of Language Variation
source.authors: Amanda Myntti; Erik Henriksson; Veronika Laippala; S. Pyysalo

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream benchmark accuracy across training-token checkpoints, which bears on V6, but it does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit the original scaling-law relationships.
record.gate_note: The paper reports downstream accuracy results by training-token count. It does not report held-out cross-entropy, parameter-count or compute sweeps, compute-optimal allocations, architecture comparisons, or fitted scaling laws. Scaling-law citations in the introduction are background, not results.
record.test_reason: This is a data-curation ablation. Every model is one fixed size (1.71B Llama) trained to 100B tokens on register-filtered data, and the study compares datasets on downstream benchmarks. Kaplan and Hoffmann appear only as background in the introduction, and Hoffmann again on data repetition. Accuracy rising between the first (2B) and last (105B) checkpoint is a within-run training curve. No relationship to tokens, parameters, compute or loss is fitted or predicted. The benchmarks were also chosen by Penedo et al. for 'monotonic signals', so the rise is partly built in by selection. None of the results bear on whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that register substantially affects benchmark performance. No single register beats the full HPLT v2 data, but some register combinations beat both HPLT v2 and FineWeb. They offer register labels as a tool for data selection and transparency, not as a statement about scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses fixed-size Llama models trained on different register-curated datasets and evaluates downstream benchmark accuracy. It does not use the original scaling-law method of fitting held-out pretraining loss across parameter, token, or compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream results vary by pretraining register and benchmark; the paper reports especially small accuracy increases on SIQA.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed 1.71B size and a fixed 100B-token budget, the pretraining data register shifts final downstream accuracy widely. It ranges from 0.358 (Lyrical) to 0.475 (HI-IN-HI-dtp-OP). Per-benchmark rises over training differ; SIQA barely moves.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining data composition (register/genre) changes downstream accuracy substantially at fixed model size and token count. Downstream gains from more tokens depend on data type and benchmark.

record.problems: The study uses English only and one model size (1.71 billion parameters); evaluation covers selected benchmarks and does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit predictive scaling relationships. The authors also note possible benchmark contamination and that their benchmarks may disadvantage some registers.
record.rows_left_out: No reported numerical aggregate-accuracy checkpoint comparisons in Table 3 were omitted. Individual benchmark curves in Figures 3 and 7–9 were not separately extracted except the SIQA trends explicitly described in Section 5.2; many figure-only values are not numerically stated.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss reported; no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fit or extrapolation to larger runs.
No compute-budget sweep or compute-optimal allocation.
Architecture and size held fixed; no shape comparison.
English text pretraining only. Data is repeated up to 5 epochs for some registers, but no scaling fit is made for repeated data.
Only one model size and first-versus-last checkpoint accuracy. No relation of downstream accuracy to scale or loss is fitted or predicted.
No exponents or fits compared across setups.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with V6 'supports' labels overreads within-run checkpoint gains as a scaling test. The evaluation benchmarks were chosen for monotonic signal, and there is a single model size with no fitted predictive relationship. I reclassified the study as cites_only/T6 and dropped all labels. The row numbers themselves match Table 3.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fit against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run loss.
No compute-budget sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation.
The model architecture and parameter count are held fixed; depth and width are not compared.
The experiments are English text pretraining; other modalities, fine-tuning, transfer, and repeated-data scaling laws are not tested.

Measures downstream benchmark accuracy across training-token checkpoints, but does not test downstream predictability from pretraining loss, model parameter count, or compute, and does not fit a predictive relationship.
No scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits are fitted or compared across methodological choices.

rows.subject: FineWeb-trained Llama model
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream benchmark accuracy between first and final training checkpoints.
rows.note: The study reports this as a downstream accuracy measure, not pretraining loss.
rows.check: Two-checkpoint (2B vs 105B tokens) weighted accuracy of one fixed-size model per dataset. The increase is real, but it is a training-progress comparison on benchmarks pre-selected for monotonic gains. It is not a test of predictable downstream scaling (V6), and no fit or prediction is made. The rows are the study's dataset comparison, not a scaling result.

rows.subject: Narrative (NA)-trained Llama model
rows.operation_detail: Compared SIQA accuracy from the first to final training checkpoint.
rows.note: The paper describes SIQA gains as very small overall and identifies this as the largest increase.
rows.check: The SIQA gain of about 0.03 over training is the largest seen on that benchmark. It is reported in the text with no baseline value. It describes a weak training-curve rise, not downstream predictability with scale or loss.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Benchmark-weighted average accuracy across the tested pretraining datasets, first to final checkpoints
reader_labels.reason: Average downstream accuracy increases in every reported dataset run; see R1–R19. These results concern training-token progression, not a fitted prediction law.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: SIQA benchmark for Narrative and Instructive-Informational models
reader_labels.reason: SIQA accuracy gains are described as very small overall, with the largest increase only approximately 0.03; see R20–R21. The study does not establish general downstream predictability from loss or model size.
